content:
The pandemic hasn't broken anything. That's the observation I keep returning to, and I think it gets lost in the urgency of the response. COVID-19 didn't break the healthcare system, or the supply chains, or the manufacturing base, or the strategic reserves. It revealed that all of them were already broken. The virus is an X-ray - it shows the skeleton, and the skeleton turns out to have fractures we've been walking around on for a very long time.

Start with the masks. Australia can't make surgical masks in sufficient quantity to supply its own healthcare workers during a pandemic. This isn't a novel discovery. The vulnerability was documented in reports, flagged in reviews, and mentioned in the sort of bureaucratic assessment that gets produced, acknowledged, filed and forgotten. We knew we couldn't make masks. We didn't build the capacity to make masks. When we needed masks, they weren't there.

That's the whole pattern in miniature, so scale it up. We can't make ventilators. We import most of our medical devices and roughly ninety percent of our pharmaceuticals. The supply chains for critical medications run through factories in India and China, and when those factories slowed in the early weeks, the medications became scarce - not unavailable, not yet, but scarce in the way that makes pharmacists anxious and health administrators do contingency arithmetic on the backs of envelopes.

The healthcare system was already running at capacity before any of this arrived, and here we reach the uncomfortable part. Efficiency means no slack. No empty beds, no idle staff, no surplus equipment. The system was optimised for normal demand and normal demand is all it can carry. When demand spikes there's nothing in reserve, because surge capacity is expensive and budgets don't fund expensive things that sit unused. We didn't fail to build it through oversight. We declined to build it, deliberately, every year, and called the decision good management.

The supply chains tell the same story. Just-in-time delivery, adopted by virtually every industry, means small warehouses and minimal inventories. Products arrive as needed rather than before. This is genuinely efficient - it lowers storage costs, reduces waste and frees up capital - and it also means any disruption translates immediately into a shortage, because there's no buffer anywhere. We optimised so thoroughly that the concept of a buffer was designed out of the system entirely.

The toilet paper business was absurd and also instructive. People saw empty shelves and panicked, which emptied more shelves, which produced more panic. Supply hadn't declined at all. Demand spiked, and the chain had no capacity to absorb a spike because it was never designed to - it was built for steady-state conditions, and steady-state conditions were what we had right up until we didn't.

**The Dependency Nobody Debated**

The digital picture became visible overnight. When offices closed and work moved online, the entire economy became dependent on video conferencing, cloud computing and collaboration platforms - all American, all operated by companies headquartered in jurisdictions that aren't ours, subject to laws that aren't ours, optimised for priorities that aren't ours.

Zoom is an American company. Teams is an American product. The servers sit in American data centres under American law. When Australian businesses, schools and government agencies moved their operations onto those platforms, they moved onto foreign infrastructure. That wasn't discussed or debated. It was simply done, because there was no alternative, because we'd never built one, because building alternatives is expensive and inefficient and the market had supplied perfectly good products from somewhere else.

Every one of these fragilities was known beforehand. The reports existed. The warnings had been issued. The lack of surge capacity had been identified, the supply chain vulnerabilities mapped, the manufacturing hollowing observed and lamented at length.

Nobody acted, and I don't think it's because the information was hidden. Acting would have meant spending money on resilience rather than efficiency, and our political system rewards efficiency because efficiency is visible. It shows up in budgets, in quarterly reports, in the metrics administrators and ministers use to demonstrate competence. Resilience is invisible by nature. It sits in warehouses, in unused capacity, in capabilities maintained and rarely deployed. You can't point to resilience on a spreadsheet. You can only ever point to its absence, and by the time you're pointing it's already too late to fix.

That asymmetry is the thing I'd change if I could change one thing. Not any particular shortage - the masks and the ventilators are symptoms, and treating symptoms is how we got here. What we need is a standing requirement that resilience appear somewhere on the page: a published national capability register naming what we can make, what we hold, how many days of it there are, and what replacement would cost in years rather than dollars. Boring, cheap, and permanent. The point isn't the document. The point is that a number nobody records is a number nobody defends, and right now the entire category of national resilience exists in no ledger anywhere.

The pandemic has produced the image and the fractures are perfectly legible in it. What happens next is the only open question.

I expect the temptation will be overwhelming to treat this as a crisis requiring a crisis response. Emergency funding, temporary measures, a period of heightened attention followed by a return to normal. The virus will be defeated or managed or accepted, the urgency will fade, and the structural weaknesses it exposed will remain untouched - because addressing them takes the sustained, expensive, politically unrewarding investment our system isn't built to produce.

We'll return to normal. Normal is the problem, and we now have the X-ray to prove it. Whether we look at it is up to us.
